item.title: Lower Limb Neural — Facilitated Positional Release (FPR) Clinical Guidance
clinicalUse: Facilitated Positional Release (FPR) is not routinely a first-choice application for Lower Limb Neural.
Use it only when examination identifies a relevant target, the clinician is appropriately trained and a safer/more direct option is not preferable.
The treatment decision must still be based on the patient's comparable sign: lower-limb neural mechanosensitivity, leg symptom distribution and function.
patientPosition: Supine, side-lying or slump sitting according to the selected neurodynamic sequence.
Start well below the symptomatic threshold.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the limb and support the leg so movement remains smooth.
stabilization: Control pelvis/trunk and change one sensitizing component at a time.
contact: Do not force a textbook contact simply to make this technique fit the region.
Position the symptomatic region toward ease and add the trained facilitating force without forcing end range.
forceDirection: Use brief low-force compression, distraction or torsion according to the trained regional setup.
Return slowly to neutral and reassess immediately.
dosage: Brief holds, often about 3–10 seconds, repeated only a small number of times before reassessment.
steps: 1. Record the exact comparable sign for Lower Limb Neural: lower-limb neural mechanosensitivity, leg symptom distribution and function.
2. Screen regional red flags, contraindications and technique-specific precautions before touching the patient.
3. Position and stabilize the patient so the target is comfortable and the manual input can be localized.
4. Confirm that this technique is genuinely relevant to the identified target; if not, choose a more appropriate regional technique.
5. Monitor pain quality, symptom distribution, guarding and patient confidence throughout.
6. Re-test the original comparable sign immediately after the trial.
7. Keep the technique only when the response is useful, then transfer the gain into active movement, loading or self-management.
mistakes: Applying the technique because it is familiar rather than because the examination supports it.
Using more force when the response is unclear or worsening.
Failing to re-test the exact movement or function that justified the treatment.
safety: Use caution with progressive neurological loss, acute nerve injury, severe irritability or red-flag spinal presentations.
Stop or modify if symptoms peripheralize, neurological status worsens, the response is disproportionate or the patient asks to stop.
item.visualCue: Lower Limb Neural assessment → correct regional setup → Facilitated Positional Release → immediate comparable-sign re-test.
